title: One sociologist kept some 90,000 index cards.
description:
One sociologist kept some 90,000 index cards. Niklas Luhmann built it up from 1952 to 1953 onwards.

He never ordered cards by topic. Each slip got a number and kept it for ever. A slip numbered 57/12 could be continued by 57/13, and an insertion became 57/12a.

He did not invent the card box. In the 16th century Conrad Gessner devised a method where notes could be rearranged at any time, and suggested gluing slips onto sheets.

He called the box a partner in communication. After more than twenty-six years he wrote that the approach was viable. He described the result as an alter ego you can talk to.

The cards were digitised and put online. Bielefeld University made them available in 2019.

The system worked because every note had a fixed address.

Sources:
- https://luhmann.surge.sh/communicating-with-slip-boxes: read (Luhmann's essay, Kuehn translation). Established that he chose a firm fixed place (Stellordnung) over ordering by topics and sub-topics; that each slip keeps its number; the example of 57/12 continued by 57/13 and supplemented by 57/12a, with 57/12a1 inside that; the phrase "after more than twenty-six years"; and that the box becomes a partner of communication and "an alter ego with who we can constantly communicate".
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niklas_Luhmann: read. Established the some 90,000 index cards, created probably between 1952 and the beginning of 1997, and that Bielefeld University digitised and put them online in 2019.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zettelkasten: read (first 39,416 of 69,624 characters verbatim). Established the start in 1952 to 1953, the unique index number in a branching hierarchy, the 2019 digitisation, and that Conrad Gessner (1516 to 1565) devised a method in which notes could be rearranged at any time and recommended gluing slips onto sheets, a step towards index cards.
